summary: RPKI manifests carry a manifest number. This Standards Track document updates RFC 9286 by specifying what issuers and relying parties should do when that number reaches its largest possible value, a case RFC 9286 did not consider.

plainLanguage.summary: A counter on a notice board eventually hits its biggest number. This says what everyone does when that happens.

questions: what happens when manifest number overflows
what is an rpki manifest number
what happens when manifest number reaches maximum
how do rpki trust anchors recover from manifest number overflow
subtitle: What RPKI issuers and relying parties do when a manifest number hits its largest possible value.

tldr.problem: RPKI manifests carry a 20-octet manifest number that must always go up. RFC 9286 says nothing about what happens at the largest value, and implementations disagree: some wait for the manifest to expire, others reject all new manifests.
tldr.mechanism: A relying party must not reject a new manifest for lacking a higher manifest number if the manifest has a different filename from the previously validated one. A CA can therefore rename its manifest to reset the counter.
tldr.outcome: A stuck CA, including a trust anchor that cannot use key rollover, can recover without issuing a new trust anchor. The RFC updates RFC 9286 and remains current.

today: RFC 9981 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2026. It updates RFC 9286 and has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: The Manifest Number Problem
sections.content:
In the RPKI, a manifest is a signed object that lists each file an issuer intends to include in its repository. Each manifest has a manifestNumber, which the issuer must increment by one whenever it issues a new manifest. Relying Parties (RPs) must check that a newly retrieved manifest has a higher number than the previously validated one (Section 4.2.1 of RFC 9286).

The field is 20 octets long, so it is bounded, and no behaviour is specified for when it reaches the largest possible value, 2^159-1. When that happens, some RP implementations accept a new manifest only after the current one has expired, and others never accept a new one.

Reaching the maximum by normal counting is practically impossible: the RFC says it would take one manifest per second for 23,171,956,451,847,141,650,870 quintillion years. The real risk is bugs or misuse, such as incrementing by large values, reissuing in an endless loop, or accidentally setting the number to the maximum.
sections.plainLanguage: A counter that only goes up will one day hit its top. Nobody will get there by counting, but a mistake could push it there by accident, and then the notice board gets stuck.

sections.title: Why Trust Anchors Are the Hard Case
sections.content:
For a subordinate CA, the fix already exists: use the key rollover process (RFC 6489) to get a new CA certificate. RPs treat the new certificate as a distinct CA, so the manifest number can be reset.

That option is not available for an RPKI Trust Anchor (TA). If a TA publishes a manifest with the largest manifest number, it is hard to rely on it afterwards. TA manifests may also have a long validity period. Issuing a new TA and distributing its Trust Anchor Locator to clients would be a lot of work for TA operators and RPs, and protection from that TA would be limited until the new locator was installed.
sections.plainLanguage: A small club can just print a fresh membership card with a new number. But the founders' original charter cannot be swapped out easily, because everyone has a copy of it.

sections.title: Resetting on a Filename Change
sections.content:
Section 2 of the RFC holds the core rule. For a given CA, an RP MUST NOT reject a new manifest for not having a higher manifestNumber if the new manifest has a different filename from the previously validated one. In effect, the RP resets its stored manifest number for that CA when the filename changes. This updates Section 4.2.1 of RFC 9286.

A CA configured to use a new filename on every issuance would make the number check pointless. So CAs SHOULD NOT use new manifest filenames except to fix the invalidity problem described here, and an RP MUST alert its operators when a manifest filename changes for a CA.

RFC 9286 requires two replay checks: a greater manifestNumber and a more recent thisUpdate. An RP following this RFC skips only the first one, momentarily, after a filename change. As long as it still performs the second check, it is protected against replay attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: If the club starts a new roll of tickets with a different name printed on it, the guard stops comparing numbers with the old roll. He still checks the date, and he tells the manager that the roll changed.

sections.title: What Counts as a Filename
sections.content:
A CA names its manifest through a Subject Information Access (SIA) entry with an accessMethod of id-ad-rpkiManifest. The manifest filename is the final segment of the path of the accessLocation URI in that entry.

A CA certificate may contain several such entries. For comparisons, an RP may use the filename from any one of the entries in the previously validated CA certificate. If that filename does not appear in any manifest entry of the certificate now being validated, the filename has changed.

So a CA with multiple entries that wants to rely on this behaviour MUST make sure none of the filenames from the previous certificate appear in the new one. Otherwise the RP may conclude the filename is unchanged and keep its stored number.
sections.plainLanguage: The filename is the name on the roll of tickets. If any old name is still printed on the new roll, the guard thinks it is the same roll and keeps comparing numbers.

sections.title: Manifest SIA Verification
sections.content:
To avoid certain forms of replay attack, RPs MUST verify that the URI in the accessLocation of one of the id-ad-signedObject access methods in the manifest's SIA extension exactly matches the URI shown in the RRDP publish element (RFC 8182) or the path presented by a remote rsync server.

If this check fails, the fetch has failed, and the RP MUST proceed as described in Section 6.6 of RFC 9286.
sections.plainLanguage: The guard also checks that the address written on the ticket matches the booth it came from. If not, he treats the delivery as failed.

sections.title: Comparison With RFC 8488
sections.content:
Section 3.2.1 of RFC 8488 describes a manifest-selection approach in which an RP collects all unexpired valid manifests for a CA and selects the one with the highest manifestNumber. The RFC states that its own approach is different from that one.

Section 6 adds general advice: RPs that meet other permanent invalidity scenarios should consider how to fix them without forcing a CA or TA to roll its key. One example is alerting the operator and offering an option to stop relying on cached data for the affected repository.
sections.plainLanguage: Another office picks the ticket with the biggest number out of the whole pile. This note takes a different route and does not copy that.

sections.title: Operational and Security Notes
sections.content:
CA software can support the reset in several ways. For example, it could change the manifest filename when the manifest number reaches a threshold, or alert the operator and ask for confirmation before changing the filename.

On security, the RFC says reliability improvements to the RPKI strengthen its dependability. To protect against replay attacks while the number check is skipped, RPs should keep verifying thisUpdate as RFC 9286 requires. The SIA check in the previous section adds protection against certain replays, and the security considerations of RFC 9286 remain relevant. There are no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: The ticket software can switch to a new roll by itself at a set number, or ask a person first. Checking the date keeps everything safe in the meantime.
